1) The first thing you want to do is establish some neural connections, let's say a habit, related to the practice. The first step is not meditation. Pick a time of day. This will only take a minute. I recommend doing this first thing in the morning since it tends to make me feel a little more energized, but do whatever works for you consistently. If you miss the time, still do it later. If you don't get around to it all day, still do it just before you go to sleep. It only takes a minute, and it will genuinely make you feel good, so it will be easy to establish a habit upon. It's just a breathing technique.

-sit or lay in a comfortable position, where your whole body can be relaxed and stable (and safe if you lose consciousness).

-inhale all the way, filling your lungs. You should do this relatively fast; faster than you normally breath, but not at a racing pace. Let's say it'll take 1.5 seconds to fill your lungs.

-exhale all the way, emptying your lungs. This should take about the same amount of time.

-repeat this inhale/exhale 30 times. While doing it, try to really be aware of your breath and how full your lungs are. It's okay if you think about other stuff too, just try to remain aware of the breathing.

-you are essentially hyperventillating, which means you're getting a serious hit of oxygen, so you might start to feel tingly all over or light-headed. That's okay and totally normal. That's it. Do this for a week, just to get used to doing this as a habit. When you can consistently do this for a week – striving for a similar time every day, feeling like you're really aware of your breath, not missing a day, then move on to the next step.

2) You'll see this technique as the most common meditation technique on the internet, but I see it as really just a basic focus exercise. Still, it is a very good starting step in this process.

-at your same time that you liked to practice your breathing technique, sit/lay in a stable and comfortable position. Set a timer for 2 minutes Close your eyes and relax your body from head to toe.

-breath in normally, without trying to consciously force it. If becoming aware of your breath has forced you to breath manually, that's okay, just do it at what seems like a normal pace.

-try to focus entirely on the breath and the act of breathing. Feel it going in through your face. Notice the sensation of it passing through your throat. Picture it filling your lungs and escaping on the exhale.

-try to focus on the breath to the exclusion of all other thoughts. You will fail this, by the way, but that's okay. When you notice that you've started paying attention to something else, just bring your attention back to your breath. Sometimes, your mind will go on whole thought adventures before you realize that you stopped paying attention to your breath. That's totally fine and normal. The important practice here is that you notice it, tell yourself that it's okay for those thoughts/feelings to be there (you're not aiming for a completely silent mind at this point), but that you are going to have your awareness let go of them and go back to the breath. It really is okay for those thoughts to be floating around your mind, but the point is to not let them grab your awareness and run with it.

-you might fail at this 100 times in a session. You might have a really solid session one day, and then fail at this twice as much for the next week. That's all fine. It's kind of like weightlifting – if you want to get good at lifting weights, you don't simply hold the weight above your head and say, “See? I can do it!” The strength comes from lifting it over and over again. Same thing with your focus and attention. Right now you're just practicing letting go of the thing that pulled your attention away without your intention, and bringing your awareness back to a specified place. Doing it over and over again is good practice, not weakness.

-eventually, you'll start to notice something. The distractions you notice won't just be big, complete thoughts. You'll start to notice subtle sensations, or incomplete thoughts, or sounds that form the basis of words but haven't quite made it into sentences, or things like that. Essentially, you'll just become aware that you are distracted by more simple things that you didn't even notice were there before. This might take a while of practice before you really become aware of it. This might feel like you're getting worse, since you're more distracted now, but this is an important step.

After you've gotten yourself to do this practice consistently, every day for a week, add another minute. Do it the next week for 3 minutes, then the next for 4, then the next for 5 minutes. If it becomes too hard to focus for that long and you can't make it the whole time, then scale back a minute and try upping it again the next week. It seems simple enough, but it really can be hard if you're not used to it, and that's okay. Once you've gotten yourself to consistently do it for 5 minutes every day for a week, then move on to the next step.

3) Here's where the real meditation starts:

(continued in the comments)

(continued from above)

-Get comfortable, stable, etc., like before. Set an alarm for 5 minutes.

-I still do #2, where I'm focusing on breathing, to start out. I only do this for a minute or so, just long enough to quiet the large thoughts and start to become aware of the more subtle things that can distract me from the breath.

-At this point, you need to let go of the breath. What you need to do now is be in a mental place where you're noticing the thoughts/emotions/perceptions that are coming from the more subtle places deeper in your mind, but not have your awareness taken by them on a journey of thought. You hear the sound patterns that normally become words, or the simple words that normally become a story, or the simple images that normally become an imagined scenario, or the body sensations that would normally become concerns, etc. - you notice them, and you let them go. They will try to grab at you and take you, but you simply let them go and continue to look deeper.

-Again, you will fail at this. Many times, they will grab you and you'll realize you spent most of the meditation in your memories of your grandma's house or wherever. When you notice this, you just realize that it's okay that these thoughts are in your mind, it's okay if they're still floating around and you can hear them, but they are only dragging your awareness around because you are grasping onto them. Then you let them go. Sometimes, out of habit, you'll notice that you started paying attention to the breath again. Just let it go. It's okay; it's good practice.

-The point is to exist in a mental space where you can practice calming yourself among the chaos of your mind, and being able to see your mind from the roots, without getting pulled away by it. You are in calmness and stillness, developing the skill of being only where you intend to be, and seeing what you intend to see without the illusions being pressed upon you by a subconscious that has always been the one truly in control of you until this point.

-Once you've done this consistently for a week at 5 minutes, up the time by 30 seconds each week. I recommend getting up to the point where you're doing at least 10 minutes a day minimum, but once you start experiencing the effects this can have on you, you'll probably have days where you want to go longer or do it multiple times. You will probably notice some of the benefits on attention, impulse control, distraction, less anxiety, etc., before you even reach the 10 minute/day mark.

-With enough time, you'll start to experience more profound benefits that are harder to explain accurately. But to give you one of the more easily explainable examples – there are times where I am meditating, perceiving the sensations that are grabbing on to me and letting them go... and it will occur to me in a very visceral way that my ideas about myself – my personality, my concerns, my memories, my general sense of what syntaxaxe is – are thoughts that are holding on to my awareness and pulling at my consciousness, and I can let them go... and then my consciousness exists for a moment in this space where “I” am part of some greater unified whole, existing outside of the space and time where I'm normally me, and the life of syntaxaxe was only a small piece of a greater machine that all works toward a bigger end than any one life. I don't really think about those words, but I feel it. That experience is deeply pleasant and relaxing, a place of euphoria even, and time can seem to stop there. It is not a danger, as I eventually come out of the meditation and am back to the life of anon. But the real benefit of such an experience is that, when I am back, the problems I had seem less emotionally intense in the greater perspective of reality, and I can work on them (as I am here to do, I don't fall into the meaningless nihilism that some are afraid will come from an ego death experience of meditation), and I can work on them without the pitfalls of stress and fear of failure. I'll go for days, really feeling that my life is a small but important piece of a well functioning mechanism that is doing exactly what it should do, a mechanism which is also me (along with everyone else), and it makes me happy to work hard and build a strong life.
Everybody's gotta find the technique that works best for them.
